```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r attach}
library(mysterymodel)
```

A clinical prediction paper reports a c-statistic. There are at least four
different quantities with that name available from one fitted model, they
differ by more than the rounding a manuscript shows, and nothing in the number
itself says which one it is. `mm_validate()` returns all of them, one per row,
labelled, so that choosing is a decision someone makes rather than a default
nobody noticed.

```{r fit}
cohort <- mm_synthetic_cohort(n = 600, prevalence = 0.11, seed = 1978)

project <- mm_project("uds", "event",
                      c("age", "bmi", "sex", "prior_uti"),
                      positive_class = 1, cohort = cohort,
                      split_var = "year", split_at = 2023,
                      cluster_id = "pid", seed = 1978)

model <- suppressWarnings(
  mm_model(project, cohort, nonlinear = "age",
           interactions = list(c("prior_uti", "sex"))))

validation <- mm_validate(model, cohort, B = 100, full_process = TRUE)
validation$metrics[, c("basis", "n", "events", "c_stat", "cal_slope",
                       "brier")]
```

## The four bases

**Apparent** is the model scored on the rows it was fitted to. It is always
optimistic, and it is reported here so that the optimism is visible rather
than absent.

**Bootstrap, fixed model** comes from `rms::validate()`. Each resample refits
the same formula, which corrects the optimism of *estimating coefficients*. It
re-derives nothing the formula was shaped by.

**Bootstrap, full process** refits the whole strategy inside every resample:
knot placement, `datadist` and factor-level handling are all learned from the
resample rather than inherited from the original fit.

**Held out** is the rows the project's split reserved, scored once.

Two cells are empty, for two different reasons, and both are the right answer.

The `brier` cell on the fixed-model row is empty because `rms::validate()`
returns Somers' Dxy and the calibration slope, not a Brier score. Carrying the
apparent Brier across into that row would make it look corrected when nothing
corrected it.

The scaled Brier gets the same treatment one step further on. It is a score
against a reference, and left alone each basis would use its own prevalence, so
a column of them would be scores against different references. Every basis here
is scaled against the development cohort's reference, reported as `brier_ref`,
and a basis with a prevalence of its own keeps that value in its `note`:

```{r brier-ref}
validation$metrics[, c("basis", "brier", "brier_ref", "brier_scaled")]
```

The `cal_slope` cell on the **apparent** row is empty because that number is an
identity rather than an estimate. Scoring an unpenalized maximum-likelihood fit
on the very rows that produced it forces the calibration intercept to zero and
the slope to one: they are the fit's own score equations rearranged. Printed
beside a held-out slope they read as the model being perfectly calibrated,
which is the one thing they cannot show. You can watch them be exactly that:

```{r identity}
y <- as.integer(model$fit$y)
lp <- as.numeric(model$fit$linear.predictors)
c(intercept = unname(coef(glm(y ~ 1, family = binomial(), offset = lp))[1]),
  slope     = unname(coef(glm(y ~ lp, family = binomial()))[2]))
```

The package detects the identity rather than assuming it, so a fitting method
that does not force it, a penalized fit for instance, would have its apparent
calibration reported as the estimate it would then be.

```{r split}
parts <- mysterymodel:::mm_split(project, cohort)
c(development = nrow(parts$dev), held_out = nrow(parts$held))
range(parts$dev$year)
range(parts$held$year)
```

One function owns the split, so fitting, validation and held-out scoring cannot
disagree about which rows are development. A row with a missing `year` falls on
neither side, and is an error rather than a silent drop.

## What the full process does and does not cover

This is the distinction the package will not let a caller skip. The detail
object names what was actually repeated:

```{r covers}
detail <- validation$full_process_detail
detail$covers
cat(detail$note, "\n")
```

`covers` is a list that will grow. Imputation, selection, tuning and
interaction screening are not re-executed, because the package does not do them
yet. A strategy including any of them is not fully validated by this function
either, and saying so in the returned object is what keeps the claim honest as
the pipeline grows.

The optimism and the correction are both available, rather than only their
difference:

```{r optimism}
round(rbind(apparent  = unlist(detail$apparent[names(detail$optimism)]),
            optimism  = detail$optimism,
            corrected = detail$corrected), 4)
```

Those two calibration numbers in the `apparent` row are the identity again, and
here they are load bearing rather than misleading: an in-sample slope that is
exactly one in every resample is what makes the optimism of the slope equal to
the mean out-of-sample shortfall, which is the quantity the corrected row
reports.

The scaled Brier in that table is derived, not differenced. It divides by
`rate * (1 - rate)` of whichever rows were scored, so an in-sample value and an
out-of-sample value are scaled by different constants and their difference would
carry that drift as well as the optimism. The Brier itself is on one scale
throughout, so it is corrected and the scaled version is then computed from the
corrected value against one fixed denominator, the development cohort's own
no-information Brier:

```{r no-information}
c(no_information_brier = detail$no_information_brier,
  corrected_brier      = unname(detail$corrected[["brier"]]),
  derived_scaled       = unname(detail$corrected[["brier_scaled"]]),
  check = 1 - unname(detail$corrected[["brier"]]) /
    detail$no_information_brier)
```

On a cohort of 150 that correction moved the reported number from -0.024 to
-0.040, so it is not a rounding matter.

Resamples that cannot be fitted are counted, not dropped quietly:

```{r valid}
c(valid = detail$valid, of = detail$B)
detail$adequate
detail$failures
```

A resample that separates, or that is missing a factor level, is a real feature
of a small cohort. An optimism averaged over the survivors of a selection
nobody reported is not the quantity it claims to be, so the count is part of
the result and `adequate` is `FALSE` when too few fitted.

## One caution about comparing the two bootstrap rows

They look comparable and are not. The fixed-model row derives its c-statistic
from `rms`'s Somers' Dxy as `0.5 + Dxy / 2`; the full-process row is a mean of
`pROC` AUCs over resamples. Two estimators of the same population quantity
differ a little by construction, so a small gap between those two rows carries
no information about the modelling strategy. Compare each against **apparent**,
which is the comparison each was built to support.

## Resampling the patient rather than the row

The cohort has repeat visits. Resampling rows treats two visits by one person
as two independent facts, and that narrows every interval it touches.

```{r resample}
dev <- parts$dev
by_row     <- mysterymodel:::mm_resample(dev, cluster_id = NULL)
by_patient <- mysterymodel:::mm_resample(dev, cluster_id = "pid")

c(rows_in_cohort = nrow(dev),
  row_draw       = length(by_row),
  patient_draw   = length(by_patient))
```

A row draw always has exactly as many rows as the cohort. A patient draw has as
many *patients*, so its row count varies with which patients were drawn, and a
patient contributing two visits brings both or neither.

Here is the property that matters, stated as a check rather than as a claim.
Take the patients with exactly two visits, and count how many rows each of them
contributes to the draw:

```{r cluster-check}
drawn <- dev[by_patient, ]
twins <- names(which(table(dev$pid) == 2L))
rows_drawn <- table(factor(drawn$pid, levels = twins))

table(rows_drawn %% 2L)
range(rows_drawn)
```

Every count is even. A patient drawn once brings two rows, a patient drawn
twice brings four, a patient not drawn brings none. No single visit is ever
separated from its sibling, which is what makes the resample a draw of patients
rather than a draw of rows wearing patient labels.

The project declares `cluster_id = "pid"`, so both bootstraps draw patients:

```{r clustered-by}
validation$clustered_by
validation$fixed_model$clustered_by
```

That second one was this package's own omission for a while, and the note used
to blame `rms` for it. `rms::validate()` passes its extra arguments through to
`rms::predab.resample()`, which takes a `cluster` and draws whole units when it
is given one, so nothing but the missing argument was stopping it.

```{r fixed-note}
cat(strwrap(validation$metrics$note[validation$metrics$basis ==
                                    "bootstrap, fixed model"], 72), sep = "\n")
```

The resample count in that note is the number `rms` actually fitted, not the
number asked for. `predab.resample()` keeps only the resamples that converged
and mentions the shortfall only when `pr = TRUE`, which `validate.lrm` leaves
off, so a corrected index can be an average over the resamples that happened
to work with nothing on the object to say so. The count comes back as the `n`
column, and falling below four fifths of `B` is reported as inadequate, the
same threshold the full-process row uses.

## Scoring any set of predictions

The metric helper that produces each row is usable on its own, which is how a
calibration or subgroup table gets the same arithmetic as the main table
instead of a second implementation of it:

```{r metrics-direct}
y <- mysterymodel:::mm_event_indicator(parts$held$event, 1)
p <- mm_predict(model, parts$held)$.pred

by_hand <- mysterymodel:::mm_metrics(p, y, basis = "held out, by hand")
by_hand[, c("basis", "n", "events", "c_stat", "c_lower", "c_upper",
            "cal_intercept", "cal_slope")]
```

Those are the same numbers as the held-out row of the main table, because it is
the same function. One column is deliberately not the same, and it is worth
seeing why:

```{r reference-differs}
held_row <- validation$metrics[validation$metrics$basis == "held out", ]
c(main_table   = held_row$brier_scaled,
  main_ref     = held_row$brier_ref,
  by_hand      = by_hand$brier_scaled,
  by_hand_ref  = by_hand$brier_ref)
```

A scaled Brier is a score against a reference, and a bare call uses the
reference of the rows it was given. The main table passes the development
cohort's reference to every basis instead, so that reading down the column
compares like with like. A subgroup table wants the bare behaviour, since
each subgroup's own skill score is the question being asked there.

## By subgroup

```{r subgroup}
held <- parts$held
held$.p <- p
held$.y <- y

do.call(rbind, lapply(split(held, held$sex), function(g)
  mysterymodel:::mm_metrics(g$.p, g$.y, basis = as.character(g$sex[1]))[
    , c("basis", "n", "events", "c_stat", "cal_slope")]))
```

Read those with the event counts beside them. A c-statistic from a few dozen
events is compatible with a wide range of truths, and the interval columns are
in the full return value for exactly that reason.

## Rows that cannot be judged

The cohort above is complete. A real external cohort is not, and the two ways
it is incomplete are not the same thing.

```{r holey}
holey <- cohort
held_rows <- which(holey$year >= 2023)
holey$bmi[1:25] <- NA                      # development, a missing predictor
holey$bmi[held_rows[1:9]] <- NA            # external, a missing predictor
holey$event[held_rows[20:27]] <- NA        # external, a missing outcome
holey$bmi[held_rows[26:30]] <- NA          # and the overlap of the two

holey_model <- suppressWarnings(
  mm_model(project, holey, nonlinear = "age",
           interactions = list(c("prior_uti", "sex"))))
holey_validation <- suppressWarnings(
  mm_validate(holey_model, holey, B = 50, full_process = TRUE))

holey_validation
```

```{r eligibility}
str(holey_validation$eligibility$held_out)
```

A patient missing a predictor cannot be scored. A patient missing the outcome
can be scored but contributes nothing to a performance estimate. They are
counted apart, with the overlap separately, because collapsing them hides which
and because the specific error worth preventing is quietly taking a missing
outcome for a non-event: that leaves the event count unchanged while inflating
the denominator, so every reported risk comes out low and nothing in the table
looks wrong.

```{r not-a-non-event}
held <- holey[holey$year >= 2023, ]
row <- holey_validation$metrics[holey_validation$metrics$basis == "held out", ]
c(rows_in_the_held_out_period = nrow(held),
  rows_scored                 = row$n,
  events_among_them           = row$events)
```

The bootstraps resample the fitted cohort and not the frame it was handed, so a
resample's composition does not depend on how much of it was missing:

```{r fitted-cohort}
c(supplied = holey_model$n_supplied,
  fitted   = holey_model$n_dev,
  resampled_by_the_full_process =
    holey_validation$full_process_detail$eligibility$n_scored)
```

And the caveat travels with the number rather than living in a methods section:

```{r caveat}
cat(strwrap(row$note, 72), sep = "\n")
```

That last sentence is the point. Complete-case analysis is a computational
strategy, not a guarantee. Missingness can be informative, the more so in a
cohort this size, so the exclusions are disclosed everywhere they apply instead
of being summarised away. Multiple imputation is the answer and is not in this
package yet; `mm_predict()` keeps refusing to put a number on an incomplete
record in the meantime.

## The honest summary

A fingerprint ties a validation result to the fit that produced it, so a table
cannot drift from its model without the pairing changing:

```{r fingerprint}
identical(validation$fingerprint, model$fingerprint)
substr(validation$fingerprint, 1, 16)
```

Report the held-out row when a split exists, the full-process row when it does
not, the apparent row beside either so the optimism is visible, and the `note`
column verbatim in the supplement.
